Clinical Reference

Hepatic Encephalopathy

On this page
A reversible neuropsychiatric syndrome of liver failure and/or portosystemic shunting — gut-derived ammonia and neuroinflammation impair astrocyte function. Diagnosis is clinical (ammonia neither confirms nor excludes it); treatment is find-and-fix the precipitant plus ammonia-lowering with lactulose ± rifaximin.
West Haven grade 0–IV Titrate lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day ~40% 1-yr survival after 1st overt episode Lactulose first-line · rifaximin add-on ≥50% episodes are precipitated
Shared

Pathophysiology

🧬

Mechanism — the story

The liver is the body's ammonia detox plant. Gut bacteria and enterocytes generate ammonia continuously — colonic bacterial urease hydrolyzes urea, bacteria deaminate protein, and small-intestinal phosphate-activated glutaminase strips nitrogen off circulating glutamine. Normally the periportal hepatocytes clear ~85% of this portal ammonia through the urea cycle. In cirrhosis, two things break at once: the hepatocytes fail, and blood is rerouted around the liver through portosystemic shunts. Ammonia floods the systemic circulation and crosses the blood–brain barrier.

Inside the brain, only astrocytes can detoxify ammonia — their glutamine synthetase fixes NH₃ + glutamate into glutamine. But glutamine is an osmolyte: it pulls water in, the astrocytes swell (the classic Alzheimer type II astrocyte), and the result is low-grade cerebral edema plus mitochondrial oxidative/nitrosative stress. Layered on top are neuroinflammation (microglial cytokines that synergize with ammonia), enhanced GABAergic tone (astrocytic neurosteroids), manganese deposition in the basal ganglia (T1-bright globus pallidus), and false neurotransmitters from aromatic amino acids. The output is a fluctuating, reversible spectrum from subtle cognitive slowing to coma.

the body is a city, the liver its sewage-treatment plant. Protein and gut bacteria make ammonia (toxic sewage); the urea cycle neutralizes it. In cirrhosis the plant is broken and the pipes reroute sewage past it (shunts) — so ammonia backs up and reaches the brain. Astrocytes are sponges mopping it up into glutamine, but the sponges swell with water and the brain "fogs." Every drug below is a different way to cut the sewage at its source or restart the plant.
Ammonia → astrocyte → HE cascade, with the exact step each drug class interrupts (teal = drug target).
The hepatic urea cycle — the ammonia-clearing machinery that fails in cirrhosis; LOLA and zinc act here.

Read the cascade left-to-right and each therapy has an address: lactulose & rifaximin cut ammonia production/absorption in the gut; LOLA & zinc restart ammonia clearance (urea cycle + muscle glutamine synthesis); PEG physically flushes the ammoniagenic bowel; BCAAs blunt the false-neurotransmitter arm. There is no drug for the astrocyte swelling itself — which is why you lower ammonia and remove precipitants.
🗂️

Classification — the four axes you name on rounds

Every HE patient is described on four axes (ISHEN / AASLD-EASL 2014): underlying cause, severity, time course, and whether it is precipitated or spontaneous.

AxisCategoriesWhat it means clinically
Type (cause)A / B / CA = Acute liver failure · B = portosystemic Bypass without intrinsic liver disease · C = Cirrhosis (by far the commonest)
SeverityMinimal → Grade IVWest Haven criteria (table below). Minimal + Grade I = covert; Grade II–IV = overt (clinically obvious)
Time courseEpisodic / Recurrent / PersistentRecurrent = ≥2 bouts within 6 months (this is the rifaximin add-on trigger). Persistent = behavioral changes always present with relapses
PrecipitantPrecipitated / Spontaneous≥50% are precipitated — always name the trigger (infection, bleed, constipation, electrolytes, meds)

West Haven Criteria (with the SONIC covert/overt overlay)

GradeClinical featuresAsterixisCategory
MinimalNormal exam; deficits only on psychometric/neurophysiologic testing (PHES, EncephalApp Stroop, critical flicker frequency, animal naming)AbsentCovert
Grade ITrivial lack of awareness, euphoria/anxiety, shortened attention span, impaired addition/subtraction, altered sleep–wake rhythm± (may appear)Covert
Grade IILethargy/apathy, disorientation to time, obvious personality change, inappropriate behavior, dyspraxiaPresentOvert
Grade IIISomnolence → semistupor, responsive to stimuli, confused, gross disorientation, bizarre behaviorPresent (if cooperative)Overt
Grade IVComa — unresponsive even to painful stimuliAbsent (comatose)Overt
Grade separates where the patient goes: covert/Grade I → clinic; Grade II → floor; Grade III–IV → ICU for airway protection. The single most useful bedside sign of the covert→overt transition is disorientation to time plus asterixis.
🩺 Clinic — outpatient optimization & prevention
Assess

When to suspect

🔍

Outpatient presentation & who is at risk

In clinic, HE is usually covert or Grade I: the family (not the patient) reports the change. Ask about day–night sleep reversal, missed appointments, near-misses while driving, and subtle personality change in a known cirrhotic. Overt features (disorientation, asterixis) mean the visit becomes an admission decision.

Symptom / sign~FrequencyWhy it happens (pathophysiology)
Cognitive slowing / inattention (covert HE)~70–80% of cirrhotics have MHEAstrocyte glutamine osmotic stress degrades processing speed and working memory before any overt sign
Altered sleep–wake rhythm (day–night reversal)~50–60%Ammonia and neurosteroids disrupt hypothalamic circadian/melatonin signaling; an early, sensitive marker
Disorientation to time / confusion~45% (overt episodes)Diffuse cortical dysfunction from cerebral glutamine accumulation + neuroinflammation; marks the covert→overt transition
Asterixis (flapping tremor)~40–60% Grade II–IIILoss of postural tone from impaired thalamo-cortical/brainstem motor drive; non-specific (also uremia, CO₂ narcosis)
Personality change / irritability / euphoria~30%Frontal-subcortical network dysfunction; GABAergic tone shift
Dyspraxia / constructional apraxia (poor figure copy)~25%Parietal-motor integration failure; basis of the number-connection and line-tracing tests
Fetor hepaticus (sweet/musty breath)~10–15%Volatile mercaptans (dimethyl sulfide) exhaled when portosystemic shunting bypasses hepatic clearance
Somnolence / stupor / coma<15% (Grade III–IV)Severe global depression of consciousness — an emergency, not a clinic problem
Scleral icterus - the visible face of the failing liver; HE rarely travels alone (jaundice, ascites, coagulopathy mark decompensation).
James Heilman, MD, Comparison of Cutaneous Jaundice and Scleral Icterus.jpg (CC BY 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Abnormal EEG - HE slows background rhythm and classically produces triphasic waves; non-specific, used mainly to exclude non-convulsive seizure.
Wikimedia Commons, Eeg CJD.jpg (CC BY 2.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Minimal HE is invisible on a routine exam but affects ~70–80% of cirrhotics, impairs driving, and predicts overt episodes. Screen symptomatic patients with a bedside tool (EncephalApp Stroop or Animal Naming Test) rather than relying on "looks fine."
Workup

What to order & when

🧪

Labs & imaging — HE is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion

CBC, CMP (K⁺/Na⁺/Cr), LFTs, glucoseEvery visit — hunt the precipitant: hypokalemia, hyponatremia, azotemia, infection, hypoglycemia all trigger HE.Initial
Venous ammoniaLow value: AASLD 2014 — "does not add diagnostic, staging, or prognostic value." A normal ammonia in a confused cirrhotic should make you doubt HE and look elsewhere. Do NOT trend it. If drawn: fasting, no tourniquet, on ice, run fast.Rarely
TSH, B12, drug/alcohol screenTo exclude mimics of altered cognition in the cirrhotic (hypothyroid, Wernicke, intoxication).If atypical
MHE testing (PHES, Stroop, CFF, animal naming)When covert HE suspected (driving concerns, work impairment, falls) — establishes the diagnosis when the exam is normal.Screening
Non-contrast head CT / MRIFirst presentation, focal deficit, trauma, or no metabolic explanation — to exclude subdural, stroke, or bleed (cirrhotics fall and are coagulopathic).If red flags
Never anchor on ammonia. If the story doesn't fit (focal signs, fever, no precipitant, first-ever episode), image the head and culture before you call it "just HE."
Treat

Chronic management

💊

Stepwise therapy — first-line → escalation

1
First-line — lactulose, titrated to stool
The anchor for treatment AND secondary prophylaxis.
▾
Lactulose reaches the colon undigested, where bacteria ferment it to lactic/acetic acid. Acidifying the lumen converts absorbable NH₃ into trapped NH₄⁺, and its cathartic effect purges nitrogen — it cuts ammonia at the source and speeds it out.
DrugStartTitrationTarget / MaxWhy it works · monitorIf intolerant / alt
Lactulose (syrup 10 g/15 mL)15–30 mL (10–20 g) PO BIDAdjust by 15 mL steps every 2–3 days to stool responseGoal 2–3 soft stools/day; maintenance 15–45 mL 2–4×/dayColonic acid trap + cathartic. Watch for over-purging → dehydration, hypokalemia, hypernatremia (these worsen HE)PEG 3350 17 g daily; lactitol where available
"More is better" is a myth — AASLD: lack of effect of a small dose is not fixed by a much larger dose. Diarrhea, cramping, and dehydration from over-dosing precipitate the very HE you're treating. Teach caregivers to titrate down for >3 stools/day.
2
Add rifaximin after the 2nd overt episode
Secondary prophylaxis — the best-documented add-on.
▾
Rifaximin is a minimally absorbed antibiotic that suppresses ammoniagenic gut bacteria and shifts microbial metabolism — it attacks the production side that lactulose only traps. Added to lactulose it cut breakthrough HE by ~58% and HE hospitalizations by half (Bass 2010).
DrugStartTitrationTarget / MaxWhy it works · monitorIf intolerant / alt
Rifaximin550 mg PO BIDNo titration needed550 mg BID (1100 mg/day) — continue indefinitely as add-onGut-selective antibiotic. Very well tolerated; not studied in MELD >25. Cost/prior-auth is the main barrierNeomycin 1–2 g/day (oto/nephrotoxic — historical); metronidazole 250 mg BID short-term (neurotoxic long-term)
Indication for rifaximin = ≥2 overt HE episodes within 6 months despite lactulose (EASL 2022 / FDA label). After a single episode, lactulose alone is standard.
3
Refractory — adjuncts, shunt intervention, transplant
When optimized lactulose + rifaximin still fails.
▾
OptionStartTitration / detailTargetWhy it worksNotes / alt
L-ornithine L-aspartate (LOLA)IV 20 g/day over 4 h ×7 d (or oral 6 g TID)Fixed courseAdjunct in refractory/persistent HEOrnithine drives the urea cycle; both feed muscle glutamine synthesis — boosts ammonia clearanceModest effect; best where lactulose/rifaximin insufficient
Zinc (sulfate)220 mg PO daily (≈50 mg elemental)Up to 600 mg/day dividedCorrect documented deficiencyCofactor for ornithine transcarbamylase + glutamine synthetaseGuideline: "cannot be routinely recommended" — reasonable if zinc-deficient
BCAA supplement~0.25 g/kg/day oralAs toleratedProtein-intolerant patientsRestores Fischer ratio, limits aromatic-AA brain influx and false neurotransmitters; also nutritionLets you keep protein intake up without triggering HE
Shunt embolization / TIPS reductionIR referralFor large spontaneous portosystemic shunt, MELD ≤11, patent portal veinRecurrent/persistent overt HERedirects portal blood back through the liver for ammonia extraction~59% HE-free at 100 d for large-SPSS embolization
Liver transplant referralRefer at 1st overt episodeMELD-Na based listingDefinitive cureReplaces the failed detox organ and abolishes shuntingRecurrent overt HE is a listing indication independent of MELD

Nutrition — the counter-intuitive cornerstone

DO NOT RESTRICT PROTEIN EASL 2022: energy 35–40 kcal/kg/day, protein 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day. Protein restriction accelerates sarcopenia — and muscle is the body's backup ammonia clearer, so restriction worsens HE. Give small frequent meals plus a late-night snack (~50 g complex carbohydrate) to shorten the overnight catabolic fast. Favor vegetable/dairy protein and BCAAs if intolerant.

Interactions

Comorbidities & drugs to avoid

⚠️

How comorbidities change the course — and the meds

ComorbidityEffect on HEManagement change
Renal failure / AKI↓ ammonia excretion + azotemia → precipitates HEAvoid nephrotoxins/NSAIDs; hold diuretics; treat AKI; may need CRRT if refractory hyperammonemia
Hypokalemia (often diuretic-induced)Drives renal ammoniagenesis and intracellular alkalosis → more NH₃Replete K⁺ aggressively; reduce diuretics; a top reversible precipitant
HyponatremiaAdds osmotic stress to already-swollen astrocytesCorrect slowly; avoid over-rapid Na⁺ shifts
GI bleed / varicesBlood is a huge protein/nitrogen load → ammonia surgeControl bleeding, transfuse, lactulose, antibiotics; a classic precipitant
Infection / SBPCytokines synergize with ammonia; systemic inflammationDiagnostic paracentesis + empiric antibiotics in every HE admission with ascites
Sarcopenia / frailtyLoss of muscle = loss of backup ammonia clearanceDo NOT restrict protein; nutrition + resistance activity; BCAAs
DiabetesAutonomic dysmotility/constipation; independent MHE riskEnsure regular bowel movements; treat constipation
TIPS / large spontaneous shuntDiverts portal blood past the liver → post-TIPS HE in ~10–50%Optimize lactulose/rifaximin; consider shunt reduction/embolization
Drugs to avoid / use with caution: benzodiazepines, opioids, and zolpidem (directly precipitate HE — the single most avoidable trigger); over-aggressive diuresis (hypovolemia, hypokalemia, alkalosis); PPIs when not clearly indicated (associated with increased HE risk via small-bowel bacterial overgrowth); NSAIDs (AKI + GI bleed). When sedation is unavoidable, use the lowest dose of a short-acting agent and monitor closely.
Monitor

Titration & follow-up

📈

What to recheck, and when

  • Stool diary — the real titration target: 2–3 soft stools/day. Review at every visit and by phone during dose changes.
  • Electrolytes / renal panel — within 1–2 weeks of a lactulose/diuretic change, then every 1–3 months; catch over-purging early.
  • Cognitive check — orientation, asterixis, and a repeat MHE test at 3–6 months in covert HE.
  • Adherence & precipitant review — constipation, dehydration, new sedatives, infections at every visit.
  • Transplant candidacy — reassess MELD-Na and refer/relist; a first overt episode is itself a referral trigger.
Prevent

USPSTF A/B & prevention

🛡️

Grade A & B screening — protect the liver upstream

HE is an end-stage complication of chronic liver disease. The highest-yield prevention is protecting and screening the liver of the at-risk patient.

GradeRecommendationPopulation
BScreen for hepatitis C virus infectionAll adults 18–79 years
BScreen for hepatitis B virus infectionAdolescents & adults at increased risk
BScreen & brief counseling for unhealthy alcohol useAdults ≥18 (drives alcohol-associated cirrhosis)
BIntensive behavioral intervention for obesityBMI ≥30 (reduces MASLD/MASH progression)

Vaccinate every cirrhotic: hepatitis A & B, annual influenza, pneumococcal, and COVID-19 — infection is a leading HE precipitant. Counsel strict alcohol abstinence.

Escalate

When to refer / admit

🚑

Red flags → ED / admission

TIPS on fluoroscopy - an intentional portosystemic shunt that relieves portal hypertension but can cause or worsen HE; refractory post-TIPS HE may need shunt reduction.
Samir, Fluoroscopic image of transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) in progress.jpg (CC BY 3.0), via Wikimedia Commons
Send to the ED / admit for: overt HE (Grade ≥II) — disorientation, marked somnolence, or coma; inability to maintain oral intake or take lactulose safely at home; a serious precipitant (GI bleed, suspected SBP/infection, AKI, marked hyponatremia/hypokalemia); first-ever episode needing a mimic work-up; or no reliable caregiver to manage titration.
Grade III–IV (stupor/coma) = airway at risk → call 911, position to protect the airway, do not force oral lactulose into an obtunded patient (aspiration).
🛏️ Wards — acute inpatient management
Admit

Who to admit

📋

Admission criteria & initial profile

Admit any cirrhotic with overt HE (Grade ≥II) that cannot be safely reversed at home. The admission is really two jobs running in parallel: lower the ammonia and find the precipitant — the second one is what actually gets them better.

  • New or worsening disorientation, somnolence, or asterixis (Grade II–IV).
  • A precipitant needing inpatient care: GI bleed, suspected SBP/infection, AKI, significant electrolyte derangement, or dehydration.
  • Cannot take/keep down oral lactulose, poor oral intake, or aspiration risk.
  • No reliable caregiver; failed outpatient management; diagnostic uncertainty (first episode, atypical features).
Grade III–IV (stupor/coma) bypasses the floor — it goes to the ICU for airway protection.

Treat

Acute management

💊

Stepwise inpatient therapy

Overt HE on the wards: treat the precipitant AND start ammonia-lowering in parallel; escalate if no response in 24–48 h.
1
Lactulose — load then titrate
Oral/NG if airway safe.
▾
DrugStart (load)TitrationTarget / MaxWhy · monitorIf can't take PO
Lactulose25 mL (≈17 g) PO/NG q1–2h until first bowel movementThen space out; adjust to stool count2–3 soft stools/day; maintenance 15–45 mL 2–4×/dayAcid trap + catharsis. Watch K⁺, Na⁺, volume — over-purging worsens HESee rung 2 (enema)
The aggressive q1–2h loading clears the ammoniagenic colonic contents fast; once stooling, back off to a maintenance rhythm targeting 2–3 stools/day.
2
Lactulose retention enema — for the obtunded / NPO patient
When aspiration risk makes PO unsafe.
▾
RouteRecipeFrequencyTechniqueWhyAlso
Retention enema300 mL lactulose in 700 mL water (1 L total)q4–6h until improvingRetain 30–60 min, left lateral / TrendelenburgDelivers the colonic acid trap without aspiration riskPEG 3350 4 L is a faster-acting alternative (HELP trial)
3
Add rifaximin + reassess precipitant
If not improving by 24–48 h.
▾

Rifaximin 550 mg PO BID as add-on (Sharma 2013: lactulose+rifaximin gave 76% vs 44% reversal and 23.8% vs 49.1% mortality vs lactulose alone). If still not responding, the answer is almost always a missed or untreated precipitant — re-culture, re-tap the ascites, recheck electrolytes and for occult GI bleed, and re-image the head. Consider PEG 3350 4 L for faster catharsis.

"Refractory HE" on lactulose is usually unrecognized SBP, a slow GI bleed, or a sedative still on the MAR — not true drug failure.
Monitor

Daily management

📈

What to trend each day

  • Mental status / West Haven grade — the primary response marker (NOT ammonia). Document orientation and asterixis each round.
  • Bowel movement count & quality — titrate lactulose to 2–3 soft stools/day; too many means dehydration coming.
  • Electrolytes & renal function — daily; replace K⁺ and Mg²⁺, watch Na⁺ and creatinine.
  • Volume status — I/O and daily weight; over-diuresis and over-purging both relapse HE.
  • Precipitant status — culture results, ascitic fluid, bleeding, and whether the offending drug is truly stopped.

West Haven grader

🧮

Grade the encephalopathy & get the disposition

Pick the highest-severity description the patient meets — it maps directly to level of care.

Grade 0 / Minimal — normal exam, deficits only on testing
Grade I — trivial unawareness, sleep reversal, short attention, mild tremor
Grade II — lethargy, disorientation to time, asterixis, personality change
Grade III — somnolent/semistupor but rousable, gross disorientation
Grade IV — coma, unresponsive to pain
—
Select a grade.

West Haven Criteria (AASLD/EASL 2014). For depth of coma also score the Glasgow Coma Scale; for prognosis/listing use MELD-Na on MDCalc and CLIF-C ACLF.

Escalate

When to call ICU

⬆️

Escalation triggers

Transfer to ICU for: West Haven Grade III–IV (stupor/coma) or a GCS ≤8 — cannot protect the airway → intubation; witnessed or high aspiration risk; hemodynamic instability / septic shock; active severe GI bleed; or ACLF with ≥2 organ failures. AASLD 2023 suggests even Grade II with clinical concern warrants closer (ICU-level) monitoring.
Dispo

Discharge & disposition

🏠

Readiness + where they go

Discharge readiness: mental status back to baseline (oriented, no asterixis); precipitant identified and treated; stable electrolytes/renal function; reliably passing 2–3 soft stools/day; secondary prophylaxis in place (lactulose ± rifaximin); and a caregiver taught to self-titrate lactulose (reduce if diarrhea, increase if fewer stools or early confusion), recognize precipitants, and keep protein at 1.2–1.5 g/kg/day with a late-night snack.

Home

Back to baseline, capable caregiver, can manage lactulose and follow-up.

Home health

Home + nursing visits for medication teaching, labs, and paracentesis coordination.

SNF

Persistent mild cognitive/functional deficit needing 24h skilled nursing, <3h therapy/day.

Acute rehab (IRF)

Deconditioned but can tolerate ≥3h therapy/day across ≥2 disciplines.

LTAC

Prolonged complex needs (failed vent wean, multi-organ recovery) >25 days.

Hospice / palliative

Recurrent HE + decompensated cirrhosis, not a transplant candidate, goals comfort-focused.
Every admission for overt HE is a prompt to (re)assess transplant candidacy — a first overt episode signals ~40% 1-year survival without transplant.
🫀 ICU — critical care & organ support
Admit

ICU triggers

🚨

When HE belongs in the unit

The unit question in HE is almost always the airway. A cirrhotic in Grade III–IV cannot protect it, and aspiration pneumonia is the main cause of death in an otherwise reversible syndrome.

  • West Haven Grade III–IV (stupor/coma) or GCS ≤8 → intubate for airway protection.
  • Witnessed aspiration or high aspiration risk with obtundation.
  • Precipitant driving instability: septic shock (incl. SBP), massive variceal bleed, ACLF with ≥2 organ failures.
  • Refractory hyperammonemia with a rising trajectory, especially if acute liver failure (Type A) is in play (cerebral edema risk).
Distinguish the substrate. Cirrhotic/ACLF HE = airway + precipitant problem; clinically significant cerebral edema/raised ICP is uncommon (~3–4%). Type A (ALF) HE is a different beast — cerebral edema is a cardinal feature (up to ~75% of Grade IV) and the ICP bundle below applies.
Monitor

Monitoring & access

🩸

Lines, labs, targets

  • Airway/neuro: continuous SpO₂ + capnography, frequent GCS, pupils; low threshold to intubate before a procedure or transfer.
  • Access: large-bore IV for resuscitation/bleeding; central line + arterial line if vasopressors or ALF; NG/OG for lactulose once airway secured.
  • Labs: CBC, CMP, LFTs, INR, lactate, glucose (q4–6h — hypoglycemia in liver failure), Mg/Phos; cultures + repeat diagnostic paracentesis; arterial ammonia if ALF (a rise >150–200 µmol/L flags ICH risk in ALF).
  • Sedation (if intubated): short-acting agents — propofol or dexmedetomidine — so you can wake and reassess neuro status; avoid benzodiazepines.
Support

Ammonia-lowering & hemodynamic support

💉

Continue the ladder — plus vasopressors for the precipitant

Keep lowering ammonia: lactulose via NG/OG (airway secured) or retention enema; switch to PEG 3350 4 L if ileus/abdominal distention (guideline-endorsed alternative); rifaximin add-on; correct hypokalemia/hyponatremia; treat the precipitant (empiric antibiotics for suspected infection/SBP).

Refractory hyperammonemia When ammonia stays high with worsening neuro status — especially in ALF or ammonia >200 µmol/L — start CRRT. Continuous modes are preferred over intermittent HD to avoid osmotic/ICP swings; early CRRT can be considered even without AKI to filter ammonia and temporize.

HE itself does not need pressors, but its precipitants (septic shock, hemorrhagic shock, ACLF) frequently do. For coexisting distributive/septic shock:

AgentReceptors / mechanismDose rangeHemodynamic effectWhen to pick
Norepinephrineα₁ > β₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min (titrate to MAP ≥65)↑SVR, mild ↑COFirst-line in septic/ACLF shock
VasopressinV₁ receptor0.03 units/min (fixed)↑SVR, catecholamine-sparing; splanchnic vasoconstrictionAdd to norepinephrine; also lowers portal pressure
TerlipressinV₁ (splanchnic)Per protocol (variceal bleed / HRS-AKI)↓ portal inflow & splanchnic vasodilationVariceal bleeding or hepatorenal syndrome
Epinephrineβ₁ = α₁0.01–0.5 mcg/kg/min↑CO + ↑SVRRefractory shock add-on
Norepinephrine's α₁-driven vasoconstriction restores perfusion pressure without the tachyarrhythmia of pure β-agonists; vasopressin and terlipressin add splanchnic constriction that also lowers portal pressure — doubly useful in the bleeding/HRS cirrhotic.
Airway

Airway, ventilation & ALF cerebral edema

🌬️

Intubate to protect the airway; ICP bundle for ALF only

Grade III–IV HE is a protect-the-airway intubation, not a primary lung problem — NIV is contraindicated in the obtunded (aspiration). Use lung-protective settings and light, short-acting sedation.

Mode
AC/VC
volume-control assist-control
Tidal volume
6 mL/kg IBW
lung-protective
PEEP
5–8
avoid high PEEP (venous congestion/ICP in ALF)
PaCO₂
Normocapnia
avoid hypercapnia; brief PaCO₂ 30–40 for ALF ICP spikes
ALF (Type A) ICP bundle — NOT for routine cirrhotic HE For raised ICP in acute liver failure: head of bed 30°, minimize stimulation; mannitol 0.5–1.0 g/kg IV bolus for established intracranial hypertension; hypertonic saline targeting Na⁺ 145–155 mEq/L in highest-risk patients (ammonia >150, Grade III–IV, AKI, or on pressors); brief hyperventilation to PaCO₂ 30–40 for emergent herniation; avoid hyperthermia. These are ALF measures — do not reflexively give mannitol to a cirrhotic with HE.
Rescue

Advanced / refractory options

⚙️

When standard measures aren't enough

  • CRRT — for refractory hyperammonemia (esp. ALF, ammonia >200) and for concurrent AKI/volume/acidosis; continuous mode preferred.
  • Shunt embolization — persistent/recurrent overt HE with a large spontaneous portosystemic shunt and preserved reserve.
  • Liver transplant evaluation — the definitive rescue; ALF with high-grade HE is a King's-College emergency-listing pathway; recurrent cirrhotic overt HE supports listing.
  • Extracorporeal liver support (MARS/albumin dialysis) — may transiently lower ammonia/improve HE grade but no consistent survival benefit; bridge/rescue only.
Downgrade

When to downgrade

⬇️

De-escalation to the floor

Step down when: HE grade has improved toward West Haven 0–I with restored airway reflexes and successful extubation; the precipitant is controlled (infection treated, bleeding stopped, AKI/electrolytes corrected); hemodynamically stable off (or weaning) vasopressors; and organ failures are resolving (ACLF grade improving). Not yet if the airway is still tenuous, ammonia is still climbing, or the precipitant is uncontrolled.
ICU disposition also means goals-of-care: a patient with recurrent high-grade HE, multi-organ failure, and no transplant path is one where palliative care belongs early — HE that keeps recurring is a marker of terminal liver disease.

Landmark trials

Trial (year)DesignResultWhy it matters
Bass — RFHE (2010, NEJM)RCT, rifaximin 550 mg BID vs placebo, n=299, 6 mo (91% on lactulose)Breakthrough overt HE 22.1% vs 45.9% (HR 0.42); HE hospitalization 13.6% vs 22.6% (HR 0.50)Established rifaximin add-on for secondary prophylaxis of recurrent overt HE. Link
Sharma (2009, Gastroenterology)RCT, lactulose vs placebo for secondary prophylaxis, n=140Recurrent overt HE 19.6% vs 46.8%Showed lactulose prevents recurrence — the basis for maintenance therapy after the first episode. Link
Sharma (2013, Am J Gastroenterol)RCT, lactulose+rifaximin vs lactulose alone for overt HE, n=120Reversal 76% vs 44%; mortality 23.8% vs 49.1%; less sepsis, shorter staySupports combination therapy for the acute overt episode. Link
Rahimi — HELP (2014, JAMA Intern Med)RCT, PEG 3350 4 L vs standard lactulose for acute overt HE, n=102Faster HE resolution (1 vs 2 days); greater 24-h HESA improvementValidated PEG catharsis as a rapid acute alternative/adjunct. Link
Als-Nielsen (2004, Cochrane/BMJ)Meta-analysis, non-absorbable disaccharidesBenefit on HE; foundation for lactulose as first-lineAnchored lactulose despite modest RCT quality. Link
LOLA (Cochrane 2018)Meta-analysis of L-ornithine L-aspartateImproves HE and may lower mortality vs placebo/no interventionSupports LOLA as an adjunct in refractory/persistent HE. Link
